transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
CNN, Politico, and MS Now's journalists are back in the White House after a five-day legal
battle that began with President Trump's decision to abruptly pull their passes.
They went to court and argued that the president violated their constitutional rights by banning
them because he was unhappy with their coverage of them.
Only this morning, a federal judge rejected the Justice Department's national security arguments.
Issued a temporary restraining order.
It did not take immediately.
Reporters were still blocked access this morning.
They went to court again, and the White House gave back the credentials.
The standoff is far from over, though.
The judge's restraining order lasts two weeks, pending further litigation.
There's still no press TV poll that typically covers Trump-linked events, like today's high-stakes
talks with visiting Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Pierce David Fochenflick has more.
I think it is just a show of resolve.
I think the president would have been very happy.
The White House would have been very happy if the other players in that television part
of the press pool, that is CBS, NBC, ABC, and Fox, which of course is owned by the president's
ally, Rupert Murdoch, had been willing to step up and said, "Well, sorry, CNN.
We'll take care of it."
That solidarity showed that it was not going to be as easy to circumvent in a way that
was acceptable to the rest of the press.
NPR's David Fochenflick reporting, "For the 14th time, the U.S. Senate has rejected
a resolution to end the war with Iran.
The House has already voted three times in favor of ending President Trump's military
action.
More Republicans have recently come out against a conflict that's linked to surging fuel prices,
including record-high costs for diesel."
The Israel-Palestinian conflict took center stage at the U.N. General Assembly this afternoon.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has just addressed the international body.
In defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just
left this hall.
Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas also addressed the U.N. General Assembly today,
but via a pre-recorded video after the United States denied the leader a visa to attend
in person.
More from NPR's Kat Lonsdorf.
It's the second year in a row that the Trump administration has denied a visa to the Palestinian
leader to attend the gathering.
In a video address in Arabic, Abbas called the refusal of his visa "unlawful and punitive."
He accused Israel of carrying out a "genocidal war" that has created an unprecedented humanitarian
catastrophe.
Israel denies that.
Abbas called for a Palestinian state with the unification of Gaza and the West Bank
and said that continued Israeli violence in both occupied territories is making that increasingly
difficult to realize.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
From Washington, this is NPR News.
AI assistants are becoming increasingly popular as the technology grows more sophisticated.
And Piers Windsor-Johnson reports...
The more an AI assistant can do, the more access it may need to things like email, calendars,
travel accounts and banking information.
Cornell University tech policy professor Sarah Krepp says problems can arise when those systems
are given too much freedom to act.
They're very literal, but they don't understand kind of the broader human intent behind it.
A mistake could mean changing a reservation, sending an ill-considered email or taking
another action before the user ever sees it.
Windsor-Johnson, NPR News.
Harmful disease outbreaks spread by wildlife are on the rise around the world, NPR's Jonathan
Lambert with details.
Humans can influence risk for diseases in lots of ways.
Cutting down the rainforest might bring people into closer contact with harmful animal viruses.
Or climate change could be pushing disease-carrying mosquitoes to new places.
But figuring out just how much influence humans have is tricky.
A new study in the journal Nature tried to answer that question by creating a big global
map.
Researchers pinpointed over 50,000 instances of someone getting diseases like Ebola, impacts
or dengue.
Then they analyzed how human activity, including deforestation and climate change, influenced
risk.
Humans influenced virtually all of these diseases, though no one factor drove them all.
But access to health clinics boosted the likelihood of detecting an outbreak.
The authors say investing in healthcare can keep an outbreak from spreading.
Jonathan Lambert, NPR News.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News.

topics.text: CNN, Politico, and MS Now journalists regain White House press credentials after five-day legal battle with Trump administration
Federal judge issues temporary restraining order in press credential dispute, lasting two weeks pending further litigation
U.S. Senate rejects resolution to end war with Iran for 14th time as fuel prices surge
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addresses U.N. General Assembly defending Israel's military actions
Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas denied U.S. visa, addresses U.N. via video calling Israel's actions genocidal
AI assistants gaining access to sensitive personal data like email, calendars, and banking information raises security concerns
Study finds human activity including deforestation and climate change influences spread of wildlife-borne diseases globally
